title: How Do Habits Form?
paragraphs: A surprisingly large proportion of what we do each day is governed not by deliberation but by habit. Routine actions such as preparing breakfast, unlocking a phone or taking the usual route to work unfold with minimal conscious involvement, conserving mental resources for situations that genuinely demand attention.

Psychologists commonly break habits down into a three-part loop: a contextual cue, a routine and a reward. Cues may be temporal, spatial, emotional or social, the routine is the behaviour itself, and the reward is whatever outcome reinforces the association and makes repetition more likely.

As the loop is rehearsed, responsibility for the behaviour appears to migrate from brain networks involved in goal-directed planning to those that support automatic responses. Once this transition has occurred, the cue can elicit the routine almost independently of the reward, which accounts for the stubbornness of unwanted habits and the limited power of good intentions to dislodge them.

Establishing a new habit is correspondingly gradual. A frequently cited study at University College London found that participants needed an average of 66 days before a daily behaviour became automatic, though the figure varied enormously between individuals. Effective approaches therefore tend to focus less on motivation and more on design: beginning with modest steps, anchoring the behaviour to an existing cue and reshaping the environment to reduce friction.
